summary: Many Internet of Things deployments use small devices that sense or control things such as in home automation or industrial systems. This proposed standard profiles TLS and DTLS for such devices, describing which features and options they should use to get secure communication with limited resources. It also covers how these profiles fit with protocols commonly used in IoT.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7925 is a checklist for securing small devices. It says which encryption suite to use for each kind of credential, how long to wait before retrying a lost packet, how to get good random numbers without a mouse or a disk, and which parts of TLS to turn off. It does not change TLS; it only chooses from what TLS already offers.

subtitle: Which TLS and DTLS 1.2 options a small, resource-limited device should use to talk securely.

tldr.problem: Small devices can rarely afford the full range of TLS options: they have little memory, slow radios and often no clock, so a general-purpose configuration is both expensive and hard to operate.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a profile of TLS 1.2 and DTLS 1.2 that picks one ciphersuite per credential type, fixes timeouts and randomness rules, and states which extensions are required, optional or forbidden. It changes nothing in TLS itself and adds no new extension.
tldr.outcome: An embedded developer can configure a TLS stack from the document alone and know what every peer will do. The profile also drops features that cost bytes or memory without helping a constrained device, such as compression and renegotiation.

today: RFC 7925 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It defines the profile of TLS 1.2 and DTLS 1.2 for constrained devices, and it relies on the cached information extension in RFC 7924 for its certificate profile.

sections.title: Why a Profile for Constrained Devices
sections.content:
An engineer developing an Internet of Things device has to investigate the security threats and decide which security services to use against them. Letting IoT devices exchange data usually requires authenticating both endpoints and protecting the data in transit for confidentiality and integrity. Those services can sit at different layers of the protocol stack, but TLS and DTLS have been widely used with application protocols and are likely to be useful for IoT scenarios as well.

Fitting Internet protocols into constrained devices is difficult, but profiles and protocols exist for it, such as the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP). CoAP messages are mainly carried over UDP with DTLS, and other transports can be used, such as SMS or TCP.

While the main goal of the document is to protect CoAP messages using DTLS 1.2, the information is not limited to CoAP or to DTLS. The document defines a profile of DTLS 1.2 and TLS 1.2 that offers communication security services for IoT applications and is reasonably implementable on many constrained devices. A profile means that the available configuration options and protocol extensions are used to best support the IoT environment. The document does not alter the TLS or DTLS specifications and does not introduce any new extension.

The main target audience is the embedded system developer configuring and using a TLS or DTLS stack, and it may also help those developing or selecting a suitable stack for an IoT product.
sections.plainLanguage: Small devices need encryption, but they cannot afford everything TLS offers. This RFC picks a workable subset: which key exchange to use, how to handle lost packets, which extensions to send. Nothing in TLS itself changes, so a device can use an ordinary TLS stack and simply configure it the way this document says.

sections.title: TLS, DTLS and the Two Communication Models
sections.content:
TLS has two layers. The Record Protocol sits on a reliable transport such as TCP and provides connection security using symmetric cryptography. The handshaking protocols consist of the handshake protocol, the change cipher spec protocol and the alert protocol, and let the two sides authenticate each other and agree on encryption algorithms and keys before application data flows.

DTLS is deliberately similar, but it runs over an unreliable datagram transport, so it must cope with the absence of reliable and ordered delivery. Three differences matter. An explicit sequence number and epoch field are included in the Record Protocol, and the value used to compute the message authentication code is the 64-bit number formed by concatenating the epoch and the sequence number. Stream ciphers must not be used with DTLS, and the only stream cipher defined for TLS 1.2 is RC4, which is no longer recommended even for TLS. The handshake protocol was extended with a stateless cookie exchange for denial-of-service resistance, adding the HelloVerifyRequest message, and the handshake message format was extended to deal with message loss, reordering and fragmentation.

The document describes two communication architectures and therefore two profiles. In the first, a constrained TLS or DTLS client talks to one or more servers. Before the handshake the client needs to know the IP address of the server and what credentials to use, which may be delivered as part of a firmware package or through a configuration protocol. The second architecture has a constrained server, for instance a device offering resources to nearby devices in a local network.

A ciphersuite bundles several choices: the authentication and key exchange algorithm, the cipher and key length, the mode of operation, the hash algorithm for integrity protection, the hash algorithm for the pseudorandom function, and miscellaneous details such as the length of authentication tags. TLS 1.2 also introduced authenticated encryption with associated data suites, where a block cipher mode such as AES-CCM encrypts and authenticates a message at once. Some of those suites have shorter authentication tags and suit low bandwidth links: TLS_PSK_WITH_AES_128_CCM_8 has an 8-octet tag where the regular CCM suites have 16-octet tags.
sections.plainLanguage: DTLS is TLS with three additions, because it runs over UDP and packets get lost or reordered: each record carries a sequence number and an epoch, old-style stream ciphers are not allowed, and the server can send a stateless cookie to check the client is real. The document then describes two situations: a small device talking to servers, and a small device acting as the server.

sections.title: Credential Types and What Must Be Known Up Front
sections.content:
The mandatory-to-implement functionality depends on the credential type. The document supports three: pre-shared secrets, raw public keys and certificates. In every case the device needs to know which algorithms to prefer and which endpoint each credential belongs to.

With a pre-shared secret, a shared secret and an identifier must be available to the device and to the other party. With a raw public key, a public key and a private key are stored on the device, and if the other end also uses raw public keys, their public key has to be provisioned out of band. With certificates, the device stores the public key as part of the certificate and the private key, and both parties are assumed to hold a trust anchor store containing CA certificates and, where certificates are pinned, end-entity certificates. Without a trust anchor store the device cannot validate a certificate.

These initial credentials are often called the root of trust. A different key pair must be provisioned for each device and installed as securely as possible, and generating the keys on the device itself is preferable to generating them outside it. A separate interaction may then configure further credentials, for example through the LWM2M protocol.

The pre-shared secret profile requires the implementation of TLS_PSK_WITH_AES_128_CCM_8. RFC 4279 requires TLS implementations to support PSK identities up to 128 octets and PSKs up to 64 octets, and this profile allows the same limits while recommending shorter identities. Identities should not assume a structured format such as a domain name or an IP address, and the server must compare them byte by byte. The client indicates which key it uses by including the PSK identity in the ClientKeyExchange message, and the Server Name Indication extension lets a server with several keys pick the right one.

The raw public key profile, which uses RFC 7250, requires TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_CCM_8. It is the first step into public key cryptography without the cost of certificates and a public key infrastructure. The certificate profile requires the same ciphersuite.

Whichever credential is used, it must be generated with care. A shared secret derived from a password or a device identifier is subject to dictionary attacks, and a lack of randomness when generating key pairs can result in the same key pair being used on many devices.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three ways for a device to prove who it is, and each one has a mandatory encryption suite. With a shared secret, the device and the server hold the same secret and the device sends a name for it. With raw public keys, the device holds a key pair and the server's public key is set up beforehand. With certificates, the device also needs a store of trusted authorities. In every case the device needs its credentials before the handshake starts, and the secrets must be chosen with enough randomness to resist guessing.

sections.title: Certificates in Practice
sections.content:
Support for the cached_info extension of RFC 7924 is required in the certificate profile. Caching certificate chains lets the client reduce the communication overhead significantly, because otherwise the server would provide the end-entity certificate and the chain with every full DTLS handshake. The use of ECC ciphersuites is restricted to the named curves of RFC 4492, with secp256r1 recommended at the time of writing and uncompressed points following the CoAP recommendation.

Service identity verification, as described in RFC 6125, is essential. The client builds a list of acceptable reference identifiers, the server provides its identifiers in a PKIX certificate, and the client matches them. The recommendations are that certificates must not use DNS domain names in the common name and must use the subjectAltName attribute instead, must not contain wildcard characters, and must not contain multiple names. Where a server node is provisioned with a fully qualified DNS domain name, the certificate must contain that name as a dNSName. For client certificates, the identifier used in the subjectAltName or in the leftmost common name component must be an EUI-64.

Neither the Online Certificate Status Protocol nor certificate revocation lists are used. Instead the profile relies on a software update mechanism to provision information about revoked certificates, and on the same mechanism to change trust anchors. Because some keys cannot be changed, manufacturer-provisioned credentials are typically used only to obtain further certificates.

The certificate content is fixed: X.509 version 3 certificates, signed with ecdsa-with-SHA256 or stronger throughout the chain, including the CA certificates. Devices must support a server certificate chain of at least 3, not counting the trust anchor, and may reject longer chains. The signature algorithms extension must be sent so that SHA-256 is selected rather than the SHA-1 default, though the extension does not apply to the pre-shared secret suite. Clients must support client certificate URLs where client certificates are used and the server is not constrained, and the trusted CA indication extension is recommended when clients talk to dynamically discovered servers.
sections.plainLanguage: When certificates are used, the chain can be cached between handshakes, which saves a lot of bytes. The rules are strict: one name per certificate, no wildcards, the name in the subjectAltName field, and a chain of at least three certificates below the trust anchor. Revocation is handled by software updates rather than by checking with a revocation server, because a small device has no room for that traffic.

sections.title: Errors, Resumption and Compression
sections.content:
TLS conveys errors through the alert protocol, with fatal alerts ending the connection immediately and warnings that an application may ignore, since many IoT devices have little way to log errors or none at all. The alert messages marked RESERVED exist only for backwards compatibility with SSL and must not be used. The certificate-related messages must not be used with pre-shared secret or raw public key authentication, and the decompression failure message must not be used because the profile does not compress. For the pre-shared secret case the server must return the decrypt_error message rather than unknown_psk_identity, since the two do the same job.

Constrained clients must implement session resumption, which reduces the number of message exchanges, the computational overhead, since only symmetric cryptography is used, and the bandwidth needed. When the server is the constrained side, the client must implement the ticket-based form of resumption in RFC 5077, which needs no per-session state on the server. If both ends are constrained, both should implement RFC 5077 and must implement basic session resumption. A client that does not want to resume can send a ClientHello with an empty session identifier to fall back to a full handshake.

Compression at the TLS or DTLS layer is not recommended, because compression algorithms add code size and complexity and are subject to attacks such as CRIME.

Perfect forward secrecy keeps past conversations confidential even if the long-term secret is later compromised. The recommended pre-shared secret suite does not offer it, because it uses no Diffie-Hellman exchange. It offers, in the RFC's words, excellent performance, a very small memory footprint and the lowest on-the-wire overhead, at the expense of using no public cryptography at all. Physical attacks on a device give an attacker access to stored key material, so an implementation that reuses the same ephemeral Diffie-Hellman keys across sessions partly defeats the property; implementations should not reuse ephemeral Diffie-Hellman keys over multiple exchanges. A client claiming support for this profile must implement the ciphersuites listed for its credential type.
sections.plainLanguage: The profile trims the error list, requires clients to resume sessions rather than start over, and forbids compression. The cheap pre-shared secret suite has one drawback: if the shared secret is later stolen, the recorded traffic can be read. The asymmetric suites avoid that at the cost of more work per handshake.

sections.title: Keep-Alive, Timeouts and Randomness
sections.content:
Middleboxes such as stateful firewalls and NAT devices keep state that expires, and packets get blocked when it does. Periodic keep-alive messages keep that state alive. The heartbeat mechanism of RFC 6520 tests whether the other peer is alive and can also be used for path MTU discovery. Whether it is worth using depends on the exchange pattern: for client-initiated one-shot messages there is no use for a keep-alive extension, and the same holds for regular data uploads, where a device is likely to sleep between transmissions. For server-initiated messages the heartbeat extension is recommended, though it may have to be coordinated with application exchanges to avoid redundant keep-alives.

Low power radio technologies limit the size of a message: IEEE 802.15.4 supports frames of 127 bytes, and SMS carries 140 bytes without concatenation. DTLS fragments a handshake message over several records so each fits in one datagram. To deal with lost messages DTLS adds timeouts and per-flight retransmissions. RFC 6347 suggests an initial timer of 1 second, doubling at each retransmission up to no less than 60 seconds, but this document recommends an initial timer of 9 seconds with exponential backoff up to no less than 60 seconds. The reason is that a spurious retransmission can make congestion worse, and a larger initial value absorbs the latency of slow devices and of networks such as GSM-SMS. Its worst case wait time is the same as with a 1 second timeout, 63 seconds, while triggering fewer retransmissions, 2 instead of 5. A sleepy node may choose a lower threshold and a smaller initial timeout, but must keep the network stability considerations in mind.

TLS needs random numbers during the handshake, and a device has far fewer sources of randomness than a laptop or a desktop, since there is no mouse movement, no timing of keystrokes and no moving disk heads. The Random structure in the ClientHello and ServerHello has two components, the current time in Unix format and a sequence of 28 random bytes. Because many devices have no accurate clock, the receiver should not assume the time value is accurate and should treat it as an opaque random string. Devices must offer a way to generate quality random numbers, either inside the microcontroller or through a dedicated crypto chip.
sections.plainLanguage: Two practical rules matter most for small devices. First, do not retry lost packets too quickly: the RFC asks for a nine second first timeout rather than one second, because a network that is merely slow should not be made slower by retries. Second, the device needs a real source of randomness, which usually means a hardware generator, because the usual sources of entropy on a computer do not exist on a gadget.

sections.title: Renegotiation, Downgrading and Key Sizes
sections.content:
Renegotiation, where an established connection negotiates new parameters, must be disabled. There is no cryptographic binding between the original handshake and the renegotiation, which is the basis of the renegotiation attack. Clients must respond to a server-initiated renegotiation attempt with the no_renegotiation alert and must not initiate one themselves.

Downgrade attacks come from a client retrying a failed negotiation with an older version. The TLS fallback signalling extension solves this in general, but the solution does not apply here because version negotiation must use TLS or DTLS 1.2 or higher. Clients must not send a version lower than 1.2 in the ClientHello and must not retry with a lower version. Servers must fail the handshake with a protocol_version fatal alert if a version of 1.2 or above cannot be negotiated, and that aborted connection is not resumable.

The document recommends that chip makers implement AES and CCM, and notes that the pieces of a ciphersuite will not all change at the same speed. It asks manufacturers to make hardware AES available to developers, to allow reuse across layers, and to keep parameters flexible: AES-CCM in IEEE 802.15.4 and Bluetooth Smart uses a 13-octet nonce while DTLS uses 12 octets, so a hardware implementation built for one is not reusable by the other. It also asks for enough headroom to upgrade to a newer algorithm over the lifetime of the product, and mentions ChaCha20 with Poly1305 as a possible future choice.

For key lengths, the table of comparable key sizes shows that a 128-bit symmetric key corresponds to a 283-bit ECC key and a 3072-bit DH, DSA or RSA key, and a 112-bit symmetric key corresponds to a 233-bit ECC key and a 2048-bit DH key. The note on these recommendations is that the 112-bit symmetric figure is chosen conservatively on the assumption that IoT devices have a long expected lifetime, such as 10 years or more, and that the recommendation refers to long-term keys for device authentication, while dynamically provisioned keys may be shorter.

Finally, false start is recommended when clients send application data first. It saves one round trip, because the data can go out once the sender has sent its own ChangeCipherSpec and Finished messages. The conditions are met by the public-key suites in the document: modern symmetric ciphers with an effective key length of 128 bits, client certificate types such as ecdsa_sign, and key exchange methods such as ECDHE_ECDSA.
sections.plainLanguage: The profile closes several doors that TLS leaves open. Renegotiation is switched off because it can be attacked. Older protocol versions are refused outright, so a client cannot be pushed back to a broken version. And the document sets a floor for key sizes, taking into account that a small device may stay in the field for ten years or more.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The DTLS handshake conveys identifiers that an on-path eavesdropper can observe. The pre-shared secret exchange reveals the PSK identity, the supported extensions, the session identifier and the algorithm parameters. When session resumption is used, individual TLS sessions can be correlated by an on-path adversary. In many IoT deployments the keying material and its identifiers are persistent for a long time, because updating software on these devices is costly.

User participation is a challenge in many deployments, since the devices are unattended even though a human provisioned them at the start, so control of data sharing and configuration has to happen at the system level rather than inside the DTLS exchange. Mutual authentication lets a server collect authentication information about the device, likely over a long period, and while strong authentication prevents misattribution it also allows strong identification. Data stored on the server side is then vulnerable to compromise, and may include personal information about the owner or about the environment the device senses.

For the communication itself, the specification prevents eavesdroppers from gaining access to the content. The pre-shared secret suite does not provide perfect forward secrecy while the asymmetric versions do, which prevents an adversary from obtaining past content once a long-term secret is compromised. No extra effort is made here to make traffic analysis harder. The presence or absence of communication may itself reveal information, and the IP header, which TLS and DTLS do not protect, reveals information about the other endpoint. Applications with such concerns need further safeguards such as dummy traffic and onion routing, which are outside the scope of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: Even with the traffic encrypted, the handshake reveals which device is talking to which server, and a device that keeps the same identity for years is easy to follow. The document says so plainly and leaves the harder privacy measures, such as padding traffic or using an onion router, to the wider system design.

items.title: Renegotiation
items.text: Disabled; clients answer a renegotiation attempt with the no_renegotiation alert.

items.title: Old versions
items.text: Clients must not offer a version below 1.2, and must not retry with one.

items.title: Compression
items.text: Not recommended at the TLS or DTLS layer.

items.title: AEAD ciphers
items.text: Required; the truncated MAC and encrypt-then-MAC extensions must not be used.

items.title: Session resumption
items.text: Constrained clients must implement it; ticket-based resumption when the server is constrained.

items.title: Server Name Indication
items.text: Required unless the client never meets a server in a hosting environment.
